opening.text: Before what I want, what we have done. VAT came off electricity bills on 1 October: about £45 a year off a price-cap bill, £850 million a year, paid for by cancelling Digital ID.

Bus fares are capped at £2 across England outside London for all of 2027, £400 million from the energy department’s budget, and disabled bus passes work at any hour from April. None of it is in your Budget.

Now the Budget. I told the House our approach would be grounded in fiscal responsibility, and I meant it. But this government exists to put life’s essentials back under public control. What kind of Budget is this?

themes.title: Cost of living
themes.purpose: Breathing space on bills, visibly, this winter.

pitch.text: Energy bills are rising again this winter. People need to feel this Budget in their pockets before Christmas, not read about it in a forecast.

themes.title: Security
themes.purpose: Defence on the NATO path; prisons that hold; borders that work.

pitch.text: The defence of our nation will always be my first priority. The Defence Investment Plan is published and £4.7 billion of it is waiting for you. I have also told the House that the worst offenders will serve their full terms, and that needs prison places.

themes.title: Rebuilding public services
themes.purpose: The NHS target, special needs, social care.

pitch.text: The waiting list is falling and the 18-week target is within reach. Special needs deficits are about to hit council reserves. And I have promised a national care service without yet finding the money for it. Choose what we rebuild first.

themes.title: Growth in every postcode
themes.purpose: Build, and be seen to build, outside London.

pitch.text: This will be a Budget that moves money and power out of Westminster. Council homes are the fair way to bring the welfare bill down. Show the country that re-industrialising Britain is real.

flagships.title: End the threshold freeze early
flagships.headline: Let income tax and National Insurance thresholds rise with prices from April 2028, three years before the plan.

delivery.text: A tax cut for every basic-rate payer, but one nobody sees on a payslip until 2028: the freeze it undoes has not happened yet.

flagships.title: Free school meals for every child
flagships.headline: Every pupil in a state school gets a free lunch, not only those whose families are on universal credit.

delivery.text: It funds a place, not a meal eaten: a fifth of pupils already entitled did not take one on census day. England only; consequentials follow.

flagships.title: Keep the £2 bus fare cap running
flagships.headline: The cap ends with 2027 unless this Budget extends it.

delivery.text: £400m buys a year of the cap at today's fare gap, outside London only, and the operators' costs keep rising.

flagships.title: Cut fuel duty by 10%
flagships.headline: About five pence a litre off, for every driver, from next April.

delivery.text: Fuel duty has not risen since 2011. A cut is felt at the pump within days, and it is paid for every year after.

flagships.title: Fund the Defence Investment Plan's gap
flagships.headline: The plan's own explainer says £4.7bn is still to be confirmed at this Budget.

delivery.text: Money is not capability: equipment programmes take years, and the plan is mostly equipment. But the commitment is already published.

flagships.title: Defence day-to-day budget up 5%
flagships.headline: About £2bn a year more for the Ministry of Defence's running costs.

delivery.text: Day-to-day money pays people and keeps kit running; it does not buy the submarines, which are capital.

flagships.title: A Justice uplift for prison capacity
flagships.headline: About £1.3bn a year more for courts, prisons and probation.

delivery.text: Prison places take years to build. Money now buys staff, maintenance and the running cost of the sentencing changes the PM has already announced.

flagships.title: A Home Office uplift
flagships.headline: About £1bn a year more for policing, borders and asylum.

delivery.text: Supporting asylum seekers cost £4.0bn in 2024-25; a settlement that falls in real terms leaves that bill to be met from elsewhere in the department.

flagships.title: Health above the Spending Review path
flagships.headline: About £7bn a year on top of a settlement already growing 2.8% a year in real terms.

delivery.text: Waiting lists fall with appointments, and appointments need staff who take years to train; money reaches the list slowly.

flagships.title: A special needs settlement
flagships.headline: About £5bn a year against council deficits the NAO puts at £4.3bn to £4.9bn.

delivery.text: 43% of councils face deficits near or beyond their reserves by March 2026. Money closes the deficit; it does not slow the 12.5% a year rise in plans.

flagships.title: A down-payment on the National Care Service
flagships.headline: About £0.8bn a year towards the fair pay agreement due in 2028-29.

delivery.text: Two million adults have unmet care needs. A down-payment funds pay before the Casey review reports; it is not yet a service.

flagships.title: Investment push
flagships.headline: Public investment up 10%: about £13bn a year more capital.

delivery.text: Capital scores against the debt rule, not the stability rule, and departments underspent their capital budgets by £9.7bn last year.

flagships.title: More council and social rent homes
flagships.headline: £3.9bn a year of capital grant for social rent.

delivery.text: Land, planning and builder capacity bind before money does; the programme's own homes arrive over a decade.

flagships.title: AI retraining programme
flagships.headline: £1bn a year to retrain people whose work automates.

delivery.text: A budget, not a costing: whether £1bn buys a programme that works is a delivery question, not a fiscal one.

flagships.title: A fiscal-devolution down-payment
flagships.headline: 2% more across the other day-to-day budgets, which is where the block grants sit.

delivery.text: Two-thirds of this line is the devolved block grants; a down-payment here reaches Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland as well as the English regions.

promises.title: The tax lock
promises.text: We will not increase National Insurance, the basic, higher, or additional rates of Income Tax, or VAT. The manifesto's words, repeated at Budget 2025.

sources.quote: Labour will not increase taxes on working people, which is why we will not increase National Insurance, the basic, higher, or additional rates of Income Tax, or VAT.

promises.title: Corporation tax capped at 25%
promises.text: We will cap corporation tax at the current level of 25 per cent, the lowest in the G7, for the entire parliament.

sources.quote: Labour will cap corporation tax at the current level of 25 per cent, the lowest in the G7, for the entire parliament.

promises.title: The two-child limit stays abolished
promises.text: Ending the two-child limit from April 2026 lifts 450,000 children out of poverty. It does not come back.

sources.quote: We are lifting 450,000 children out of poverty with the end of the two-child limit.

promises.title: The fiscal rules
promises.text: We will abide by the fiscal rules, ensuring we retain a buffer to protect us against uncertainty. The Chancellor's own words to the Treasury Committee.

sources.quote: we will abide by the fiscal rules, ensuring we retain a buffer to protect us against uncertainty and the impact of instability in the Middle East

promises.title: Defence on its path
promises.text: 2.5% of GDP, then 3% in the next Parliament, then 3.5% by 2035. The defence budget does not go backwards.

sources.quote: the UK has committed to reach 3.5% of GDP on defence spending by 2035

promises.title: The triple lock
promises.text: The state pension rises each year by the highest of earnings growth, prices or 2.5%. That is the government's policy and the OBR's forecast assumes it.

rvfrz-early.text: Good. It is the one thing in the last Budget people still feel. But it is £8bn a year by 2029-30, so I will want to know what pays for it.

ufsm-all.text: Every child. I like that a great deal, and so will the party.

bus-cap.text: People in Bolton and Bury will notice that more than anything else in the Red Book.

fuel-cut.text: Drivers will thank you and the Treasury will not. Fuel duty has not gone up since 2011; be sure you can afford to keep it that way.

dip-gap.text: That is not a favour to the Defence Secretary. It is a commitment we have published.

defence-uplift.text: Day-to-day money for defence is people. Yes.

prisons.text: I have told the House the worst offenders will serve their full terms. That promise needs cells.

borders.text: Bring the asylum bill down and the whole department breathes.

nhs-above-sr.text: Eighteen weeks is the promise people remember. Protect it.

send-settlement.text: Councils are about to hit the wall on this. Yes, and quickly.

care-downpayment.text: I have waited twenty years to hear a Chancellor say that.

invest-push.text: Build. But remember the debt rule watches investment even when the stability rule does not.

council-homes.text: Council homes bring the welfare bill down. That is the argument; make it.

ai-retraining.text: Good. Make sure the North sees it, not just the Treasury.

devolution-downpayment.text: Power and money out of Westminster. That is the whole point of us.
